1.pericope_label: Haman’s house given to Esther, and his signet ring to Mordecai

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that confiscation of goods necessarily followed a sentence of death in the East, as with ourselves a convicted felon’s property is forfeited to the Crown; and of the ring he says it constituted Mordecai Vizier, one who would thereby authenticate a royal decree and, having for the time what amounts to a free hand, would save his master all further trouble. Mordecai’s position had now become what Daniel’s had been to Darius, that nobler servant to a worthier lord, since he was the queen’s cousin and had once been the means of saving the king’s life, so that he starts under distinctly favourable auspices. Keil and Delitzsch add that the house of Haman undoubtedly means the house with all that pertained to it, that by the gift of the ring Mordecai was advanced to the post of first minister, and that the king’s seal gave the force of law to royal edicts, the seal taking the place of the signature.

Henry turns the transfer into a meditation on property: thus is the wealth of the sinner laid up for the just, and what Haman would have done mischief with Esther will do good with, since estates are to be valued as they are used. The stewardship shows the vanity of laying up treasure upon earth, for he that heapeth up riches knows not who shall gather them, not only whether he shall be a wise man or a fool but whether he shall be a friend or an enemy; and with what little pleasure, indeed with what constant vexation, would Haman have looked on his estate could he have foreseen that the man he hated above all men should have rule over all that wherein he had laboured. It is our interest, therefore, to make sure of those riches which will not be left behind. Of Mordecai he finds him so humble and modest a man, and so far from being ambitious of a place at court, that though Esther had been four years queen he had concealed his relation to her and her obligations to him as her guardian, and never made use of her interest for any advantage of his own; who but Mordecai, he asks, could have taken so little notice of so great an honour?

Clarke explains that the king’s seal was in the ring, so that giving it to Mordecai was tantamount to giving him the seal of the kingdom, constituting him what a lord chancellor is among us. Wesley marks the double justice of the grant, that the goods were justly forfeited to the king and no less justly bestowed by him on the queen, to compensate the danger to which Haman had exposed her; and of Mordecai he notes that Esther had now told how nearly he was related to her, which till this time she had wisely concealed, and that he was admitted into the king’s presence and family and, as it seems, made one of the seven princes.

Gill quotes the Targum, which spells out the inventory as the men of his house and all his treasures and all his riches; and of the ring he adds what it meant socially, that with the Persians it was a token of the strongest affection and strictest friendship, the Targum calling it his signatory ring, with which he signed laws, edicts, letters and patents, so that Mordecai was hereby made keeper of the seals.

debates.question: What office did the ring confer?

positions.view: The seal of the kingdom — what a lord chancellor is among us
The vizierate: power to authenticate decrees, a free hand that saved the king all further trouble
The post of first minister, the seal standing in place of the royal signature
Keeper of the seals, the ring being also a Persian token of the strictest friendship

outliers.claim: Alone in reading the confiscation as a lesson on property, and alone in dwelling on how long Mordecai had kept his kinship with the queen to himself.
Alone in comparing Mordecai’s new standing with Daniel’s under Darius, and in noting what favourable auspices he began under.

themes: On that day did the king Ahasuerus give the house of Haman the Jews’ enemy unto Esther the queen
And Mordecai came before the king; for Esther had told what he was unto her
And the king took off his ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it unto Mordecai
And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman

3.pericope_label: Esther pleads for her people, and the king bids her write what the law cannot unwrite

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that Esther’s work was only half done: she had seen her race’s foe condemned and her kinsman exalted, but the royal edict still stood, and being sealed with the king’s seal was supposed beyond the possibility of alteration; it was not a case in which Mordecai’s new dignity would authorise him to interfere, so Esther, the ice once broken and her courage grown, appeals afresh to the king to do what theoretically lay beyond his power. He finds considerable skill in the wording of her request, since she avoids speaking of the king’s letters and calls them the device of Haman, which he wrote, while the injury done is laid at the king’s own door, in the destruction of Jews in all the king’s provinces. Of the king’s answer he reads the motive coolly, that Esther’s device is seen through and he shrinks from so decisive a step as revoking a decree once issued, so does what he can instead: give any orders you please about them, short of repealing the former order. Keil and Delitzsch put the legal difficulty plainly, that the chief enemy was destroyed but the edict, having been issued in due legal form, could not according to the laws of the Persians and Medes be revoked.

Henry weighs the manner of the asking. She came a second time uncalled into the king’s presence, encouraged again by the golden sceptre held out to her, and fell at his feet and besought him with tears, every tear as precious as any of the pearls with which she was adorned, for it was time to be earnest when the church of God lay at stake. Let none be so great as to be unwilling to stoop, he adds, nor so merry as to be unwilling to weep, when thereby they may serve God’s people; and he notices which petition drew the tears, since we read of none when she begged for her own life, but now that she was sure of that she wept for her people, and tears of pity are the most Christ-like. On the constitution he turns indictment: that no law could be repealed once it had passed the royal assent is so far from bespeaking the wisdom and honour of the Medes and Persians that it bespeaks their pride and folly, since it is ridiculous for any man to pretend to such infallibility as to foresee all the consequences of what he decrees, and unjust to claim such power as to make his decrees irrevocable whether those consequences prove good or bad. This savours of that old presumption which ruined us all, that we will be as gods; much more prudent is the proviso of our own constitution, that no law can be made unrepealable, since it is God’s prerogative not to repent, and to say what can never be altered.

Wesley reads the same prudence in the wording that Ellicott does, that she takes the hatefulness of the action off the king and lays it upon Haman, who had for his own ends contrived the whole business and circumvented the king in it. Clarke states the workaround the king found: whatever had passed the royal signet could never be revoked, and no succeeding edict could repeal a preceding one, but one of a similar nature might be enacted, and so the Jews be enabled legitimately to defend themselves, placed on an equal footing with their enemies.

Gill accounts for the piled-up conditions of the petition, that this heap of phrases, all signifying much the same thing, is used to work upon the king’s affections and to show how submissive she was to his will.

debates.question: How is the irrevocable law to be judged?

positions.view: It bespeaks pride and folly, not wisdom and honour: no man can foresee all the consequences of what he decrees, and it is God’s prerogative alone to say what can never be altered
It stands, and must be worked round: a second edict of like tenor can place the Jews on an equal footing with their enemies
The king shrinks from revoking a decree once issued and does what he can short of it
The edict was issued in due legal form and by Persian and Median law simply could not be revoked

outliers.claim: Alone in turning the Persian constitution into a political argument against unrepealable law, and in grounding that argument on the divine prerogative not to repent.
Alone in reading the petition as a piece of rhetorical craft that keeps the king’s own seal out of the indictment while making the injury his.

themes: And Esther spake yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet, and besought him with tears
let it be written to reverse the letters devised by Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite
For how can I endure to see the evil that shall come unto my people?
Write ye also for the Jews as it liketh you, in the king’s name, and seal it with the king’s ring
for the writing which is written in the king’s name, and sealed with the king’s ring, may no man reverse

9.pericope_label: The counter-decree written, sealed and sped to the provinces

schools.summary: Ellicott dates Sivan from the new moon in May, so that rather more than two months had passed since the first edict went out, and glosses the officers addressed as satraps. Of the couriers he renders the posts literally as the runners and the mules as horses of great speed, and offers two readings of the disputed pair of words: with Gesenius, mules the offspring of royal mares, or with Rawlinson, riders upon coursers of the king’s stud, offspring of high-bred steeds. On the substance of the grant he insists that so far as the edict authorises anything the Jews are not permitted to take the initiative but merely to stand on the defensive; as it was, it risked civil war in all the cities of the empire, though the results were lessened by the numbers who took the hint the second edict so obviously presented. Of the licence to plunder he notes that when the storm actually came the Jews declined to take advantage of that part of the edict.

Wesley reads the two-month interval as discipline: all that time God suffered the Jews to lie under the error of this dreadful day, that they might be the more thoroughly humbled for the sins under which they lay, that they might be convinced of their folly in the many offers they had had of returning to their own country, by which dispersal they had become an easy prey while their brethren in Judea could better preserve themselves, and that his goodness might be the more illustrated in so unexpected a deliverance. On the hardest clause he allows the custom but doubts the practice, holding the mention of little ones and women added to strike the greater terror into their enemies, and observing that we read nothing in the execution of any slaughter of women or children, nor is it probable that men so indulgent as not to meddle with the spoil would have killed innocent children. Clarke admits that what the beasts were is difficult to say: the word rendered mules signifies a swift chariot horse, the second is probably Persian but perhaps incurably corrupted, and the third means the sons of mares and is supposed to signify mules bred between the he-ass and the mare. There is so much confusion here, he concludes, and so little consent among learned men, and the true knowledge of them is of so little importance, that we may rest contented with the names our translations give; they were, no doubt, the swiftest and hardiest beasts to be had. On the terms he argues parity: they are the same words as in Haman’s decree, so the Jews had as much authority to slay their enemies as their enemies had to slay them, and since women and children stood in the former grant they must stand in this one.

Henry fastens on the languages the decree was published in. It was to be drawn up and sent out in the respective tongues of all the provinces, and from that he turns a question on his own readers: shall the subjects of an earthly prince have his decrees in a language they understand, and shall God’s oracles and laws be locked up from his servants in an unknown tongue? Of the expedient itself he draws the political moral, that it laid the king under a necessity of enacting a civil war in his own dominions, so that both sides took up arms by his authority and yet against it.
Gill notes that the letters were written in the king’s name and sealed with the king’s ring, which gave them authority and made them irreversible in their turn.

debates.question: Were women and children really within the grant?

positions.view: Yes, necessarily: the terms repeat Haman’s decree word for word, and women and children stood in that
The clause was added to strike terror; nothing in the execution records any such slaughter, and men who refused the spoil would hardly have killed children
So far as the edict authorises anything, the Jews may only stand on the defensive — and they declined even the plunder

outliers.claim: Alone in turning the multilingual publication of a Persian edict into a reproach against keeping Scripture in an unknown tongue.
Alone in working through the three disputed words for the couriers’ beasts and then declaring the whole question not worth settling.

themes: Then were the king’s scribes called at that time in the third month, that is, the month Sivan
unto every province according to the writing thereof, and unto every people after their language
sent letters by posts on horseback, and riders on mules, camels, and young dromedaries
the king granted the Jews which were in every city to gather themselves together, and to stand for their life
So the posts that rode upon mules and camels went out, being hastened and pressed on by the king’s commandment

15.pericope_label: Mordecai in royal apparel, the Jews in gladness, and many of the people turning Jews

schools.summary: Clarke guesses at the blue and white as stripe interchanged with stripe, takes the great crown of gold for a large turban ornamented with gold and jewels, and identifies the fine linen with the byssus of the ancients, supposed to be the tuft growing from the side of a very large muscle found on the Mediterranean coasts, of which a pair of gloves is kept in the British Museum. Of the conversions at the end he judges them worthless: these were a species of converts not likely to bring much honour to true religion, though the sacred historian states the simple fact, and they professed Judaism for fear of the Jews, whether they continued steady in that faith or not. From this he turns to his own argument, that it is only the Gospel which will not admit of coercion for the propagation of its doctrines, being a spiritual system propagated only by spiritual influence. Wesley credits the city with better motives than Ellicott allows, that not only the Jews but the greatest number of the citizens rejoiced, men who by the law of nature abhorred bloody counsels and took complacency in acts of mercy.

Ellicott is exact about the dress, noting that the word for crown here is not the one used of a royal crown and that the garment is the inner tunic, the king’s own being purple striped with white. Of the city’s joy he will allow no credit at all: the tide of royal favour had changed, and the people of Shushan were evidently not very different from any populace, who shout with the winning side; nothing succeeds like success, and the crowd of Susa cheered Mordecai as it would doubtless have hooted had it seen him led to execution. Keil and Delitzsch agree with Gill that light stands figuratively for prosperity, and locate the honour in the joy the inhabitants of Susa showed at the prevention of the threatened destruction; and of the conversions they refuse to settle the matter so fast as Clarke does, holding that the turning of many heathen to Judaism must not be explained only, with Clericus and Grotius, as a change of religion undertaken to procure security and the queen’s favour.

Henry sets no store by the robes except as evidence: these things are not worth notice but as marks of the king’s favour and the fruit of God’s favour to his church, and it is well with a land when the ensigns of dignity are the ornaments of serious piety. He takes Shushan to have been sensible of its own advantage in the preferment, not only pleased with the advancement of virtue but promising itself better times now that so good a man was entrusted with power, since when the wicked perish there is shouting and when the righteous are in authority the people rejoice. He adds what the distress contributed to the joy, that had they not been threatened they would have had no occasion for such extraordinary gladness, so that God’s people are sometimes made to sow in tears that they may reap the more joy, the suddenness of the turn adding much to it, so that they were like those that dream. On the conversions he allows both motives and adds a third: they thought the Jews great, and counted those happy who were among them, and they thought them formidable, and counted those miserable who were against them; but the holy cheerfulness of those who profess religion is itself a great ornament to it, and it was when the Jews had joy and gladness that many became Jews.
Gill reads the light as prosperity opposed to the darkness of their adversity, or else as lightsomeness and cheerfulness of spirit.

positions.view: Because it saw its own advantage in a good man’s preferment, and because when the righteous are in authority the people rejoice
Because most of the citizens abhorred bloody counsels by the law of nature and took complacency in acts of mercy
Because the tide of royal favour had turned: the crowd cheered Mordecai as it would have hooted had it seen him led to execution
Nothing much: converts from fear, not likely to bring honour to true religion — and only the Gospel admits no coercion at all
More than mere prudence: they must not be explained only, with Clericus and Grotius, as a bid for security and the queen’s favour
Mixed: some thought the Jews great and some formidable, but it was their holy cheerfulness that invited others in

outliers.claim: Alone in turning the forced conversions into an argument about the nature of the Gospel, that a spiritual system can be propagated only by spiritual influence.
Alone in reading the city’s joy as the fickleness of any crowd rather than as a verdict on Mordecai.

themes: And Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal apparel of blue and white, and with a great crown of gold
and the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad
The Jews had light, and gladness, and joy, and honour
the Jews had joy and gladness, a feast and a good day
And many of the people of the land became Jews; for the fear of the Jews fell upon them
